design_detail: Exploratory phase 2, single-site, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding pilot (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396) at the Los Angeles Biomedical Research Institute at Harbor-UCLA, February 2014 to April 2017. Twelve autistic adults with marked to very severe social anxiety (LSAS of 60 or more) were randomized to MDMA (8, in two dose subgroups of 4) or an inactive lactose placebo (4) in two blinded 8-hour experimental sessions about a month apart, with three 60- to 90-minute preparatory sessions (including mindfulness skills adapted from dialectical behavior therapy) and three integrative sessions after each; primary outcome the change in LSAS total from baseline to one month after the second session, rated by one blinded independent rater; follow-up 6 months after the last session, when the blind was broken (open-label sessions for the placebo group not reported). Sponsored and funded by MAPS, organized by MAPS PBC, with additional private donors.
can_establish: Whether, in 11 analysed autistic adults with severe social anxiety, two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy were followed by a larger fall in interview-rated social anxiety than the same psychotherapy with an inactive placebo, with a very imprecise estimate; and which acute reactions and vital-sign changes were more frequent with MDMA in 8 people.
cannot_establish: How large any effect of MDMA is, or whether it differs from participants knowing their allocation (they guessed correctly in 22 of 23 sessions) or from expectation; whether a dose matters (4 per subgroup, pooled in the paper); durability beyond 6 months; rare harms; or effects in autistic people with intellectual disability, those under 21, those with prior MDMA use, or those not physically healthy or psychologically stable, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Internet advertisements, word of mouth and clinician referrals, mainly online; advertisements were placed in autism forums and community outreach was used to limit self-selection and expectancy from drug-interest forums (Methods › Screening, eligibility, and participants, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph). Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 49 preliminary telephone screens, 25 excluded, 24 assessed in person, 12 excluded, 12 enrolled and randomized.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 or older; LSAS of 60 or more; autism confirmed with the ADOS-2 Module 4; MDMA-naive by self-report; physically healthy and psychologically stable; full criteria only in the supplement, not read (Methods › Screening, eligibility, and participants, 1st paragraph). One MDMA participant was found after randomization to have been enrolled with hypertension and a pre-study substance use disorder within the exclusion window and was withdrawn (Fig. 1 footnote; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.3 (SD 8.8); 10 men and 2 women, both women in the MDMA group; 6 White, others Latino/Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, Middle Eastern or mixed; 25% non-heteronormative sexual orientation; baseline LSAS 69 to 125; earlier psychotherapy in most (psychodynamic 10 of 12); earlier antidepressants 7, stimulants 4, anxiolytics 3; lifetime C-SSRS positive ideation 7, serious ideation 1, suicidal behaviour 2 (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2).
sample.attrition: One of 8 MDMA participants withdrawn as ineligible after randomization; the remaining 7 and all 4 placebo participants completed the primary assessment and the 6-month follow-up; their baseline scores were kept and missing data were not imputed (Fig. 1; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers able to engage with online advertisements, mostly men, aged 21 or older, without prior MDMA use, and willing to take MDMA in a trial; the authors note possible self-selection and expectancy effects (Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded experimental sessions (arrival about 09:30, drug about 10:30 after progressive muscle relaxation, end late afternoon) in a room designed to reduce sensory distress, with a pair of therapists; participants went home with a study support partner and returned next morning for integration; seven daily telephone checks after each session (Methods › Experimental sessions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Post-session follow-up, 1st paragraph; Safety monitoring, 1st paragraph). MDMA was synthesized by David Nichols at Purdue University and compounded with lactose into capsules identical to the placebo (Methods › Trial design, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: one MDMA subgroup (4) received 75 mg at the first session and 100 mg at the second, the other (4) 100 mg and 125 mg; placebo was lactose of equivalent weight; no participant declined the dose increase; no supplemental dose is described (Methods › Trial design, 2nd paragraph). The subgroups were pooled for analysis (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants had to be MDMA-naive by self-report, which could not be verified; drug screens at baseline and before experimental sessions; Table 2 lists polysubstance dependence, alcohol abuse and substance use among comorbid diagnoses in single participants (current or past not stated); concomitant psychiatric medicines during follow-up could have affected 6-month outcomes (Results › Demographics; Table 2; Discussion › Limitations, 5th paragraph). One MDMA participant who had stopped escitalopram about 2 months earlier showed no physiological or subjective response although MDMA was found in plasma (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Inactive lactose placebo with the same psychotherapy (Methods › Trial design, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 2:1 (8 and 4); the randomization procedure and allocation concealment are not described in the main text (a randomization monitor is thanked in the Acknowledgments). Baseline LSAS 91.8 (15.8) on MDMA vs 83.3 (11.9) on placebo; both women in the MDMA group (Tables 1 and 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; expectations were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported by group beyond Table 2's comorbidity lists.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS, 24-item semi-structured interview) by one independent rater at baseline, 1 day, 2 weeks and 4 weeks after each experimental session and at 6 months. Secondary (exploratory, descriptive): BDI-II, Perceived Stress Scale, Interpersonal Reactivity Index, Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, STAI, TAS-20, TASIT, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire. Vital signs before and hourly for 6 to 7 hours after dosing; adverse events, spontaneously reported reactions during sessions and for 7 days, C-SSRS at the start and end of treatment days, hourly subjective units of distress (Methods › Trial design, 3rd paragraph; Assessments; Pharmacodynamic measures; Safety monitoring).
outcomes.validity_norms: LSAS severity bands used in Table 3: 0 to 54 normal, 55 to 65 moderate, 66 to 80 marked, 81 to 95 severe, 96 or more very severe (Table 3 footnote d); response defined post hoc as a fall of 20 points or more, from prior LSAS studies (Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: a larger fall in LSAS total from baseline to one month after the second session on MDMA than on placebo, by independent-samples t test; Cohen's d for an independent-groups pretest–posttest design (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed for the two inferential tests (primary endpoint and 6-month follow-up); the eight secondary measures were presented descriptively (in the supplement, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants, therapists and the independent rater were described as blind; the single rater never attended experimental sessions and participants were asked not to reveal their beliefs; the rater's guesses were not recorded. Participants guessed wrongly in only 1 of 23 sessions (one of eight placebo sessions); the two therapists guessed wrongly in 2 and 1 of 8 placebo sessions and in 2 of 15 MDMA sessions each (Results › Blinding, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: LSAS change −44.1 (SD 14.8) on MDMA (n = 7) vs −19.3 (18.8) on placebo (n = 4); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, 95% CI of the difference 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted Cohen's d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874). Six months: −47.7 (14.7) vs −23.3 (18.0); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036, CI 1.92 to 47.01; d 1.1 (−0.31 to 2.53) (Results › Clinical response, 1st paragraph; Table 3). Editors' calculations from the printed means and SDs: difference 24.8 points, t(9) = 2.44, P = 0.038, CI 1.8 to 47.8; an approximate 95% CI for d = 1.4 of 0.04 to 2.76. LSAS fall of 20 points or more: 6 of 7 on MDMA vs 2 of 4 on placebo (Table 3). Registry, by dose: 75/100 mg change −51.0 (8.19), 100/125 mg −39.0 (17.57), placebo −19.3 (18.77).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted change scores (baseline LSAS 4 to 8 points higher on MDMA).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396: first submitted 6 December 2013, posted 11 December 2013, before the actual start (11 April 2014); a dose-finding phase 2 pilot; registered primary outcomes: LSAS total at one month after experimental session 2 and its change from baseline; no secondary outcomes registered; results posted 14 October 2020, reported by dose group. The paper pools the two dose groups and lists eight secondary measures (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The dose-group results, the point of a dose-finding design, are not reported in the paper (only in the registry, where the lower-dose group improved more); the eight secondary measures are reported only descriptively in the supplement (not read); outcomes of the placebo group's open-label MDMA sessions are not presented.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a pilot of 12 (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With 7 analysed on MDMA and 4 on placebo, interview-rated social anxiety fell by about 44 points on MDMA and 19 on placebo one month after the second session (difference about 25 points, 95% CI about 2 to 48), and the difference was similar at 6 months. Participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions. MDMA raised blood pressure, pulse and temperature during sessions and was followed more often by anxiety, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, headache and low mood; there were no serious adverse events. In the registry, the lower-dose group improved more than the higher-dose group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the trial "demonstrated rapid and durable improvement in social anxiety symptoms" and calls the effect size very large (Abstract › Results and Conclusions), although the printed interval of d includes zero. The Limitations conclude that double-blinding with an inactive placebo was adequate because one participant and both investigators made incorrect guesses (Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph), whereas participants were right in 22 of 23 sessions. The Discussion says long-term follow-up failed to detect any deleterious outcomes (Discussion, 8th paragraph) on 11 people, and the Conclusions say feasibility and safety were successfully established. The authors do acknowledge that observable drug effects may contribute to efficacy and that the sample limits claims (Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 4th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Danforth et al., Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry: rationale and design of this trial (on the project's evidence map; not read).
Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov (14 October 2020), by dose group.

replication.where_it_stands: One pilot trial of 12 people. The project's evidence map lists a completed trial in social anxiety disorder without autism (NCT05138068; protocol Lear et al., 2023) and a completed laboratory study in autistic adults with posted results (NCT04053036), neither with a publication among the sources read.

funding.funder: Sponsored and funded by MAPS, a 501(c)(3) non-profit; MAPS PBC, wholly owned by MAPS, organized the trial; additional private funding from Richard S. Ross, Lars Skovlund, The Betsy Gordon Foundation, Frances Vaughn and Angeles Arrien (Funding information).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Alicia Danforth and Charles Grob received research funds from MAPS PBC as clinical investigators; Allison Feduccia, Lisa Jerome and Amy Emerson were salaried full-time employees of MAPS PBC; Berra Yazar-Klosinski was a salaried full-time employee of MAPS; Nick Walker was paid by MAPS as an independent consultant (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Four of eight authors were sponsor employees; the sponsor's staff monitored the data and a sponsor statistician reviewed the analysis (Acknowledgments). The registry now names Resilient Pharmaceuticals as sponsor. The paper's Crossref record carries no correction or retraction (read 2026-10-17).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered randomized trial in autistic adults with social anxiety, comparing MDMA with an active placebo within the same psychotherapy, with prespecified dose arms, measured expectancy, a blinding check of participants and raters, and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: The method of randomization and allocation concealment is not described in the main text; baseline differences in 12 people (LSAS 91.8 vs 83.3; both women in the MDMA arm) are compatible with chance.

One MDMA participant was enrolled in breach of the exclusion criteria and withdrawn; participants were almost all aware of their allocation, which could change how they engaged with the psychotherapy; two needed an extra preparatory session.
One of 8 in the MDMA arm (12.5%) has no outcome, after post-randomization withdrawal for ineligibility; no imputation or sensitivity analysis; in a trial of 12 a single participant matters.

The LSAS was given by one blinded rater, but it scores participants' own reports of fear and avoidance, and participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions; knowledge of allocation could plausibly have influenced the reports. The rater's blinding was not checked.

Prospectively registered with the LSAS as primary outcome, but the registry reports it by dose group while the paper reports only the pooled comparison, and the registry's posted denominators do not match the paper's.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The overall judgment is high because the primary outcome rests on participants' reports while their allocation was evident in almost every session, and expectancy was not measured; other domains add concerns in a trial of 12. The trial can be cited for the observed LSAS changes with their wide interval, for the acute reactions and vital-sign changes seen in 8 people given MDMA, and for the absence of serious adverse events; it cannot be cited for the size of an effect of MDMA, for dose, or for durability or safety beyond this small group.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 49 telephone screens, 25 excluded, 24 assessed in person, 12 excluded, 12 randomized (4 placebo, 8 MDMA); one MDMA participant withdrawn for enrolment with hypertension and a pre-study substance use disorder within the exclusion window; 4 placebo and 7 MDMA participants completed the primary assessment and the 6-month follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image, with footnote); Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, LSAS total: placebo 83.3 (SD 11.9) at baseline and 64.0 (13.3) one month after the second session, change −19.3 (18.8); MDMA 91.8 (15.8) and 46.4 (15.2), change −44.1 (14.8); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, CI 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: difference 24.8 points (CI 1.8 to 47.8, t(9) = 2.44); approximate CI for d 0.04 to 2.76. MDMA n = 7 after baseline (Table 3 footnote c).

key_findings.finding: Six-month follow-up: placebo 60.0 (17.4), change −23.3 (18.0); MDMA 42.9 (20.4), change −47.7 (14.7); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036, CI 1.92 to 47.01; d 1.1 (CI −0.31 to 2.53); within the MDMA group, primary endpoint to 6 months t(6) = 1.117, P = 0.307.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3

key_findings.finding: LSAS fall of 20 points or more at the primary endpoint: 6 of 7 (85.7%) on MDMA vs 2 of 4 (50.0%) on placebo in Table 3; the text gives 6 of 8 (75%) vs 2 of 4. Severity at the primary endpoint: 5 MDMA participants and 2 placebo participants in the normal range.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding: participants guessed their allocation wrongly in one of 8 placebo sessions and in none of the 15 MDMA sessions (right in 22 of 23); one therapist was wrong in 2 of 8 placebo and 2 of 15 MDMA sessions, the other in 1 of 8 and 2 of 15. One MDMA participant had no physiological or subjective response (MDMA confirmed in plasma) and both investigators guessed placebo.

Vital signs: mean peak systolic blood pressure (P = 0.021), pulse (P = 0.015) and temperature (P < 0.001) higher on MDMA; maximum pulse 114 bpm and maximum temperature 37.7 °C; no systolic pressure above 180 or diastolic above 110 mmHg; values back to pre-drug levels by session end without intervention.

Reactions during the two blinded sessions, MDMA (n = 8) vs placebo (n = 4): anxiety 6 (75.0%) vs 1; difficulty concentrating 5 (62.5%) vs 1; fatigue, headache and sensitivity to cold 4 (50.0%) each vs 0 to 1. Over the next 7 days: fatigue 5 (62.5%) vs 2, headache 5 (62.5%, one severe) vs 1, difficulty concentrating 4 (50.0%) vs 0, low mood 4 (50.0%) vs 2, lack of appetite 3 (37.5%) vs 0. No serious adverse events.

Psychiatric adverse events from the first session to the primary endpoint, MDMA vs placebo: depressed mood 2 (25.0%) vs 0; suicidal ideation 2 (25.0%) vs 1 (25.0%), pre-existing in medical history; anxiety, depression, panic attack and panic reaction 1 each on MDMA; moderate events on MDMA included anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and panic attack; positive suicidal ideation occurred during two MDMA sessions and resolved by the next day.

Registry results by dose group (LSAS one month after session 2): 75/100 mg 34.3 (10.41), change −51.0 (8.19); 100/125 mg 55.5 (11.47), change −39.0 (17.57); placebo 64.0 (13.34), change −19.3 (18.77); posted denominators 4, 4 and 3. Registered 6 December 2013, before the start on 11 April 2014; no secondary outcomes registered; no serious adverse events or deaths; other adverse events in 1 of 4, 4 of 4 and 1 of 4, to the end of stage 2 (about 10 months).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures; Results › Outcome Measures, Adverse Events
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: weighting the two dose groups by 3 and 4 reproduces the paper's pooled MDMA values (46.41 and −44.14); the posted denominators of 4, 4 and 3 do not.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: small sample and wide range of scores; too small to compare doses; inactive placebo with observable drug effects, which might contribute to efficacy; prior MDMA abstinence could not be verified; undisclosed drug use and concomitant psychiatric medicines during follow-up could affect 6-month outcomes; possible self-selection and expectancy from recruitment.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages for the MDMA group mix denominators of 7 and 8: in Table 3 the primary-endpoint severity categories give 5 (71.4%) normal but 1 (12.5%) moderate and 1 (12.5%) marked, and the change categories give 4 (57.1%), 2 (28.6%) and 1 (12.5%); in Table 4 low mood and thirst are 2 (28.6%) while anxiety is 6 (75.0%), and 7-day irritability is printed as 1 (25.0%) in the MDMA column (1 of 8 is 12.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite counts with their denominator rather than the printed percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: The rate of a 20-point LSAS fall on MDMA is 6 of 8 (75%) in the Results text but 6 of 7 (85.7%) in Table 3 and the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The printed interval for the placebo-subtracted d at the primary endpoint (−0.074 to 2.874) includes zero, although the t test gives P = 0.037 and the interval of the raw difference (1.92 to 47.87) excludes zero; the editors' approximate interval for d is 0.04 to 2.76. The abstract calls d = 1.4 very large without noting its width.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Results › Clinical response, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The standardized effect is extremely imprecise; cite the raw difference with its interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 41.67% of participants had generalized anxiety disorder and 66.67% a history of depression, while Table 2 lists generalized anxiety in 2 (16.6%) and 'anxiety' in 4 (33.3%); Table 2's 'Other' pre-study medication total is 2 (16.6%) although the groups show 0 and 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comorbidity description is internally inconsistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's posted results give the primary outcome by dose group with denominators of 4, 4 and 3 (placebo 3), while the paper analyses 7 MDMA and 4 placebo participants; the placebo values are the same in both. Weighting the dose groups 3 and 4 reproduces the paper's pooled values (editors' calculation), so the registry's denominators appear mislabelled. The registry also shows the lower-dose group improving more (−51.0) than the higher-dose group (−39.0), which the paper does not report.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Results › Outcome Measures); PMC HTML (Table 3; Methods › Statistical analysis)
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's pooled result is consistent with the registry's subgroup data; there is no sign of a dose–response in these tiny groups.

reporting_issues.issue: One participant randomized to MDMA had been enrolled despite exclusion criteria (hypertension and a recent substance use disorder), found only after randomization; the analysis that leaves this participant out is labelled intention-to-treat.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Fig. 1 footnote; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3 footnote a)
reporting_issues.consequence: A modified intention-to-treat analysis of 11 of 12 randomized; screening missed an exclusion in 1 of 12 enrolled.
